newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria plans court for press, says minister.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria plans court for press, says minister.

text.p: Nigeria's military government is planning to set up a press court to try journalists that report untruths, according to information minister Walter Ofonagoro.
"The press court will be made up of journalists like you working under a judge," Ofonagoro said on Friday night at a new year party he hosted for editors and other media executives.
"There must be a built-in mechanism for checking recklessness and since it takes too long in normal courts to decide cases of libel the press court will be a faster way of getting justice," he added.
Nigeria's military government has always accused the press of peddling rumours and falsehood.
A spokesman for the press criticised the plan to set up a special court for the media.

"We oppose the proposed press court," Sam Amuka-Pemu, publisher of Vanguard newspapers, said in response to Ofonagoro's address. "We think the judicial system is adequate to take care of press excesses."

The rift between the authorities and the press has worsened since June 1993 when Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, slipped into crisis as a result of the annulment of a presidential poll by a previous military government.

Wealthy businessman Moshood Abiola, himself the owner of several newspapers and magazines, who is widely believed to have the annulled poll, has been detained since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president.
Since the election crisis, the Nigerian media has been polarised along ethnic lines like the rest of nation.
Several journalists are in detention while four were imprisoned in 1995 over an alleged plot to topple the government in a coup d'etat.
